5.text: SUMMER CLOTHING. — The Chukchee have no special summer garments,

6.text: properly speaking. Indeed, there is little need for them in those latitudes.

7.text: Fur clothes are used all the year round; the old, half-worn clothes, which are

8.text: of little use in the coldest season, being worn during the summer months.

9.text: Dampness and rain are much more destructive to fur clothing than the dry

10.text: snows of winter. So the Chukchee, who in mid-winter is clad in clean and

11.text: handsome furs, in the summer wears the worst clothing he has. Even the

12.text: well-to-do reindeer-breeders then look exceedingly shabby. The people, who

13.text: have accustomed themselves to severe cold, apparently consider it not worth

14.text: while to prepare for the milder, damp weather of the short summer months.

15.text: In the summer-time coats are worn either single or double. If single,

16.text: they are always worn with the hair side in. Among the Reindeer Chukchee,

17.text: trousers and shoes are made of strongly smoked tent-covering (retteˊm), which

18.text: has the advantage of not shrinking after having been wetted.¹ The trousers

19.text: have the usual cut. The soles of the boots are made of hard thong-seal hide.

20.text: The boots often have small guards around the front to keep the toes from

21.text: being hurt by striking against stones and roots that lie exposed during the

22.text: summer. These shoes are worn with thick grass insoles, but without socks.

23.text: They fit the foot closely, so that when walking ankle-deep in the numerous

24.text: bogs and mountain brooks, very little water can remain in the shoe. The

25.text: soles, moreover, are pierced with two rows of small holes made with a bodkin,

26.text: to facilitate the outlet of the water. Even after a long walk through water,

27.text: when a stretch of dry ground is reached, the shoes dry very rapidly under

28.text: the pressure of the foot. As there are no stockings inside, the feet will be

29.text: quite dry in half an hour’s time.

30.text: The summer trousers and boots of the Maritime Chukchee, as has been

31.text: noted before, are made of seal-skin, which is much more suitable for this pur-

32.text: pose than any kind of reindeer-skin. The seal-skin is curried and the epidermis

33.text: is left on, or the skin is well scraped and blackened with soot. Thanks to the

34.text: thickness and oiliness of seal-skin, they are nearly impervious to water.

35.text: The typical boot reaches to the knee (Fig. 181, a), and has clumsy, rather

36.text: full legs. The large soles are crimped around the edge. This latter process

37.text: is quite similar to that used by the American Eskimo. Since the Asiatic women

38.text: have no special boot-sole creasers, they use their teeth for this purpose.

39.text: The Koryak women have small ivory knives which are similar to the

40.text: boot-sole creasers of the Alaskan Eskimo; but, curiously enough, they do not

41.text: use them in boot-making, but only for tracing patterns on soft curried leather,
